So when I was VP Marketing at Adobe Sign / EchoSign we closed our first big deal with Cisco Systems.  And then … another one.  We weren’t much bigger than that ourselves, just 15 employees!
It wasn’t always easy.  But what worked well was going up to see the customers.  Meeting face-to-face.  Going to see them, getting them to try us out for free.  Building relationships.
And more importantly, being responsive to their needs.  Being flexible enough to work around their issues, and get things done.
A few years later, we had 50+ employees and were doing $10m in revenue.  A VP of Sales joined us who’d been a top rep at Salesforce.com, and he came with his playbook.  He said you could do most of the discovery remotely via email, send over a proposal, and then schedule time for Q&A before closing.  That’s exactly what we did back in the day when we sold Enterprise Edition, because it’s what we learned from Salesforce.
But it didn’t really scale down to SMBs.  In fact, in the early days, many SMB prospects wouldn’t answer emails!  So we went back to old-fashioned phone calls, and getting folks on Zoom together.
Fast forward to today, I’ve invested in dozens of SaaS start-ups, especially smaller ones (<$1M-$5M in ARR).  What I’ve seen is that while larger teams have advantages, there’s no magic here.
Many successful start-ups have gone on to close seven-figure deals without huge teams behind them. They’ve built strong partnerships by focusing on the core principles of excellent customer service, technical prowess, and relationship-building.

To succeed in selling to a CIO, you need to speak their language, understand their priorities, and be prepared to address their concerns. Here are some essential aspects of the social contract:

1. **Value proposition**: Clearly articulate the unique benefits your solution offers over existing solutions or manual processes. Be prepared to demonstrate how your product addresses specific pain points and drives tangible results.

2. **Scalability**: As a startup, you must showcase your ability to scale and adapt to meet the needs of large enterprises. This may involve providing flexible pricing models, ensuring robust infrastructure, or demonstrating compatibility with existing systems.

3. **Security and reliability**: Enterprise customers require high levels of security, data integrity, and uptime guarantees. Ensure your solution meets or exceeds industry standards for data protection, compliance, and disaster recovery.

4. **Partnership approach**: Building trust and rapport with your prospect involves showing genuine interest in their business goals and challenges. Foster open communication channels, collaborate on pilot projects, or offer customized demos tailored to their specific requirements.

5. **Flexibility and openness**: Large organizations often have complex procurement procedures, including lengthy RFP processes, multiple stakeholders, or rigorous evaluation criteria. Be adaptable and transparent throughout the sales cycle, and maintain a willingness to negotiate terms and conditions.

By grasping the intricacies of the social contract between buyer and seller, your eight-person startup can effectively compete against more established players. Focus on building strong relationships, addressing critical concerns, and showcasing your unique strengths – then watch as even the most skeptical CIOs begin to see the value in your innovation. And after $600m, growth re-accelerated again. Why would that be? Well, a lot of it is because Monday is going much, much more enterprise than before. It’s doubling down on bigger deals and bigger customers. And that takes time. You’ll see below, that’s where all the growth really is now.
At $400m ARR, Monday Is Still Growing Almost 95%, With 20% Free Cash Flow Margins
Even at $400m ARR, Monday.com still grew a stunning 94.8%!  At least, that’s what I’m calculating. They were doing about $240m in revenue in Q4’21, and likely around $300m in Q1’22. Monday is hyper-efficient though, and even with this insane growth, had already hit 20% operating margins (!). That’s crazy efficient! Monday Was “Downturn” Proof Even Before Covid
This next point will make some folks a bit uncomfortable but is important nonetheless. As you can see above, Monday’s growth didn’t slow materially during either the last downturn (2016/17), nor the current one. What did happen is a massive shift to bigger customers.
